curriculum.title: Module 1: Network Overview and Interface Concepts

chapters.title: Why This Module Comes First
chapters.content:
Network is how the appliance connects to cables, hands out addresses, answers names and chooses a path. The firewall, which decides what may use those paths, is a separate set of pages. Almost every later page in Network, Firewall and VPN stores the name of an object created here, so an error made on this screen surfaces much later as a DHCP scope, a zone or a route that looks correct and still passes nothing.

A packet moves through the appliance in a fixed order:

**Physical port → Device (bridge / VLAN / bond) → Logical interface (address) → Route or Multi-WAN**

DHCP then numbers the other hosts, DNS resolves names to those addresses, and a static route or Multi-WAN chooses the next hop.

> **Important:** The address you are using to view the admin UI is the one that can lock you out. Interface apply keeps a confirmation window for exactly that reason. Confirm only after the page loads on the new address.

chapters.title: Learning Objectives
chapters.content:
After completing this module a candidate can:

1. Distinguish the four object kinds on the Network → Interfaces screen and state the single job of each.
2. Decide, for any new requirement, whether to create a bridge, a VLAN, a bond, a VRF, a second address or nothing at all.
3. Configure a logical interface with the correct protocol for a LAN, a provider circuit and a bridge member port.
4. Explain the relationship between a logical name, a device name and a prefix, and name which other page stores which of the three.
5. Apply an interface change safely using the confirmation window, and distinguish it from the Firewall confirmation window.
6. Read an interface row after apply and translate what it shows into the fault that produced it.
7. Work through the standard eight-point interface troubleshooting sequence in order.

chapters.title: The Four Object Kinds
chapters.content:
Open Network → Interfaces. Four kinds of object appear on this screen. Each has a single job. Picking the wrong kind is the usual root cause of a configuration that reads correctly and forwards nothing.

| Kind | Example | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical port | eth0, eth1 | A socket on the appliance. Once the port is a member of a bridge or a bond, the address no longer lives on the port — it lives on the logical interface. |
| Device | br-lan, eth0.10, a bond | The thing packets are actually sent on: a bridge, a VLAN, a bond, or a bare port. |
| Logical interface | lan, wan, guest | The name every other page uses. It binds a device, a protocol and an address together. |
| VRF | cust1 | A separate routing table. Ports assigned to it use that table and leave the table that holds the office default gateway. |

> **Rule of thumb:** If a form asks for an interface, give it the logical name such as lan. If it asks for a device or a port, give it br-lan or eth0. lan and br-lan are a pair, not the same object.

**3.1 Which page stores which name**

These names are copied into other pages. Renaming an interface leaves those pages on the old spelling until each one is edited, which is why the shipped names lan and wan are normally left alone.

| Page | What it stores |
| --- | --- |
| Firewall zone | The logical interface, such as lan |
| DHCP scope | The device, such as br-lan |
| DNS listener | The logical interfaces that answer client lookups |
| Multi-WAN link | The logical WAN name, such as wan |
| Static route | The logical interface used toward the next hop |
| Traffic shaper | The device the pipe is attached to |
| Captive portal | The LAN to intercept, or a free port already out of every bridge |
| VPN local network | A prefix, such as 192.168.99.0/24 |

chapters.title: The Reference Topology
chapters.content:
Every module in this program reuses the same office. Learn these numbers now; later modules assume them without restating them.

| Role | Port | Device | Logical interface | Address |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Office desks | eth0, eth1 | br-lan | lan | 192.168.99.1/24 |
| Fiber circuit | the ISP port | that port | wan | DHCP; public example 203.0.113.10 |
| Guest (added later) | eth2 | br-guest | guest | 192.168.70.1/24 |
| Servers (added later) | tagged on the uplink | eth0.10 | servers | 192.168.50.1/24, host 192.168.50.10 |
| Branch site | — | — | — | Public 203.0.113.20, LAN 192.168.64.0/24 |

Nothing in this table is a firewall rule. An address makes the appliance present on a network; permission is decided by the Firewall pages.

> **Warning:** The WAN port stays out of br-lan. If the ISP port is found inside the office bridge, remove it before any other project — otherwise the internet circuit and the desks are one switched network.

chapters.title: Devices: Bridge, VLAN and Bond
chapters.content:
A device is what packets are sent on. Three kinds are built on this appliance, and each answers a different question.

| Device | What it does | Build it when | Key constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bridge br-lan | Turns several ports into one network. Members hear the same broadcasts and share one address placed on the logical interface. | Several sockets should be one LAN, or a new LAN needs its own broadcast domain on a free port. | A port belongs to one bridge only. Moving it moves every host on that socket. |
| VLAN eth0.10 | A tagged network on a port that already exists. Each tag is a separate device with its own logical interface and address. | One cable must carry several networks, and the switch at the other end tags them. | The ID is 1–4094 and must match the switch. The same parent uses each ID once. |
| Bond | Uses two or more ports as one link toward a switch or another appliance. The address sits on the bond's logical interface. | Two cables run to the same switch and should act as a single uplink. | Every member must first be free of any bridge and of any logical interface of its own. |

**5.1 Bridge versus bond — the distinction candidates get wrong**

A bridge connects hosts to each other. A bond connects this appliance to one other switch over more than one cable, as one link. Two cables to the same office switch are therefore a bond, or two members of br-lan. A new subnet, by contrast, is for hosts that need their own broadcast domain.

**5.2 Tagged and untagged on one cable**

The untagged network is the logical interface on the port or on the bridge — in the reference office that is lan at 192.168.99.1/24 on br-lan, and eth0 can be a member of that bridge. The tagged network is eth0.10, logical interface servers, at 192.168.50.1/24. Sharing a cable leaves them as two separate networks.

chapters.title: VRFs: Routing Tables, Not Policy
chapters.content:
A VRF is a routing table with a name. Ports assigned to it look up routes in that table, and they leave the table that holds the office default gateway. The WAN default route stays in the main table.

| Question | VRF | Firewall zone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What does it decide? | Which routing table is consulted | Which packets are allowed |
| Typical use | A customer, lab or circuit whose routes must stay out of the office table | A guest LAN that needs the internet: a zone plus a forward to wan |
| Does creating it change the other? | No. Creating a VRF leaves firewall zones untouched | No. A zone does not move a route into another table |

A VRF has a name and a table id from 1 through 4294967294. Pick an id that is free and avoid any table already listed, because Multi-WAN keeps tables of its own. The documentation uses cust1 with table 204 on port eth3 as the worked example, on the condition that 204 is not already in use. Unassign the port before deleting the VRF.

chapters.title: Logical Interfaces
chapters.content:
A logical interface is the name of a network the appliance participates in. This is where a device, a protocol and an address are bound together. It is also the object that Firewall zones, DNS listeners, Multi-WAN links and static routes select.

**7.1 Protocols**

| Protocol | You type the address | You type a gateway | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Static | Yes | On a WAN. Empty on a LAN | Office, guest, DMZ, VLAN, or a provider static handoff |
| DHCP | No | The provider sends it | Cable or fiber handoff |
| DHCPv6 | No | The provider sends it | An IPv6 handoff; LAN assignment length is separate |
| PPPoE | No | The session installs it | A provider that requires an account |
| None | No | No | A port that is only a bridge or bond member |

Tunnel protocols may appear in the list because the platform knows them, but VPN tunnels are configured under the VPN menu, which adds the interface its service needs.

**7.2 The fields that decide behaviour**

| Field | On lan | On wan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | lan — leave the shipped name; other pages already refer to it | wan |
| Device | br-lan | The ISP port, which stays out of br-lan |
| Protocol | Static | DHCP, PPPoE or static |
| IPv4 address | 192.168.99.1 | 203.0.113.10 when static; learned otherwise |
| Netmask | 255.255.255.0 | The provider mask, often a /30 or /29 on a static handoff |
| IPv4 gateway | Empty | The provider router, such as 203.0.113.9 |
| DNS | Empty, or a resolver for the appliance itself | Peer DNS, or a list you type |
| Use default route | Off | On, for the circuit that owns the internet |
| Metric | Cleared | Lower on the primary circuit |

> **Important:** Empty means removed. Clearing the IPv4 gateway removes the previous gateway. Clearing DNS removes the previous DNS list. Clearing the metric removes the previous metric. On a LAN, all three stay empty — a gateway left on lan is how the office interface ends up trying to own the default route.

**7.3 Addressing details worth knowing**

- A logical interface can hold more than one IPv4 address. The first is the primary; each extra address carries its own mask. This is the supported way to answer on two prefixes during a renumber.
- IPv6 uses a prefix length, such as 2001:db8:99::1/64. Leave the IPv6 address empty until a real prefix has been issued — a guessed address will miss the provider prefix. The IPv6 assignment length field is what hands a slice of a learned WAN prefix to a LAN.
- The appliance address is also the gateway handed to PCs and the URL of the admin UI on that LAN, so keep it outside the DHCP pool.
- A prefix published to a peer is a VPN local network, an IPsec traffic selector or a static route — never an interface address.

**7.4 Masks seen in practice**

| Mask | Prefix | Hosts | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 255.255.255.0 | /24 | 254 | Office, guest, DMZ |
| 255.255.255.128 | /25 | 126 | A LAN being split |
| 255.255.255.248 | /29 | 6 | A small public block |
| 255.255.255.252 | /30 | 2 | A provider link: your address and their gateway |
| 255.255.0.0 | /16 | Far too many for one office | Leave this mask off a LAN |

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Object
chapters.content:
Work down this table and stop at the first row that matches the requirement.

| You are trying to | Create |
| --- | --- |
| Give the office or a WAN an address | A logical interface on the device that already exists |
| Plug two sockets into the same LAN | Nothing new — add the port to br-lan |
| Start a LAN that must stay off the office broadcast domain | A new bridge, then a new logical interface, then a zone |
| Carry a second network on a cable the switch already uses | A VLAN, then a logical interface on that VLAN device |
| Use two cables as one uplink to a switch | A bond, then a logical interface on the bond |
| Keep a port's routes out of the office table | A VRF, then assign the port |
| Reach a prefix on the far side of a router you can already reach | A static route |
| Learn prefixes from another router | The Routing menu (a later product surface) |
| Hand addresses to PCs | A DHCP scope, after the logical interface exists |
| Let a remote laptop in | A VPN, after wan has a reachable address |

chapters.title: Staged Edits and the Confirmation Window
chapters.content:
Interface edits are staged. Nothing moves packets until Apply, and Apply loads the new network and then starts a confirmation window. Reload the page on an address you still have, then confirm. If the new address is wrong, wait the window out and the previous design returns.

| Behaviour | Consequence for the administrator |
| --- | --- |
| Save without Apply | The list still shows the previous address. Nothing has changed on the wire. |
| Apply without confirming | The window expires and restores the previous design. |
| Reboot during the window | The change is not rolled back. The new design stays in place even if it cannot be reached. |
| Interface window vs Firewall window | Two separate windows. When both are pending, confirm the interface first from a path that still works, then apply the firewall. |

> **Caution:** Taking lan down, or changing its address to a prefix the browser sits outside of, is the classic way to lose the admin UI. Apply from a session that can survive the change, or move a second PC onto the new address before confirming.

chapters.title: The Safe Build Order for Any New Network
chapters.content:
1. Create the device — bridge, VLAN or bond. Apply and confirm.
2. Create the logical interface on that device. Static address, empty gateway on a LAN. Apply and confirm.
3. From a host on that network, ping the appliance address. If this fails, stop. DHCP and firewall work only on top of a device that already answers.
4. Add the DHCP scope, using the device name. Apply DHCP.
5. Add the firewall zone and the forwards intended. Apply the firewall and confirm that window too.
6. Add a DNS name if people should reach the host by name.

The guest walkthrough in the product documentation follows exactly this order: br-guest on eth2, then logical guest at 192.168.70.1/24, then zone guest with a forward to wan, then DHCP on device br-guest.

chapters.title: Reading the Interface List and the Eight-Point Fault Sequence
chapters.content:
**11.1 What a row means after apply**

| What you see | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| An address in the network you typed | Static configuration is installed |
| An address you did not type, plus a gateway | DHCP or PPPoE succeeded |
| A device name and no address | The port is present and the protocol has not obtained an address, or the protocol is none |
| A gateway on lan | The office interface is claiming the default route. Clear the gateway and leave Use default route off |
| The same network on two rows | Two interfaces overlap. Move one |

Note that a WAN which is up and a WAN which is allowed by policy are two different facts. This page answers the first; the Firewall pages answer the second.

**11.2 Troubleshooting sequence — stop at the first failed check**

| # | Symptom | Cause and action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The list still shows the old address | The edit was saved but not applied, or the confirmation window rolled it back. |
| 2 | The admin UI no longer loads on the old URL | The LAN address moved. Use the new address, or wait for the window. A reboot during the window keeps the new address. |
| 3 | The WAN row has no address | No DHCP offer, a failed PPPoE username, or the WAN cable is in br-lan. Check the device name before touching firewall policy. |
| 4 | The WAN has an address but no gateway | Use default route is off, or the provider sent none. Internet traffic has nowhere to go and Multi-WAN will show a link that cannot carry traffic. |
| 5 | Two interfaces list overlapping networks | Give one of them its own range, for example guest at 192.168.70.1/24. |
| 6 | The gateway is outside the interface network | The route stays uninstalled. Fix the mask or the gateway so they share a network, as 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.9 do on a /30. |
| 7 | Clients still use the old gateway | The interface changed but the DHCP scope kept the old prefix, or PCs have not renewed. Renew a lease before calling it a firewall fault. |
| 8 | A VPN or port forward targets the old public address | Update the endpoint host, the SSL public host, or the DNS name. The current value is the address on wan. |

**11.3 Four conditions for reaching the appliance UI**

All of the following must be true at once before a desk PC loads the admin UI at 192.168.99.1:

1. lan is applied and confirmed, device br-lan, address 192.168.99.1, mask 255.255.255.0.
2. The PC is plugged into a member of br-lan. The WAN port is somewhere else.
3. The PC's address is inside 192.168.99.0/24, or DHCP on br-lan has handed one out.
4. The PC's gateway is 192.168.99.1 when it needs to leave the LAN. On the same LAN, an address in that prefix is enough.

chapters.title: Guided Laboratory Exercises
chapters.content:
Perform these on a lab appliance or inside an approved maintenance window. Keep a second PC on the office LAN as the confirmation path throughout.

**Lab 1 — Document what already exists (20 minutes)**

1. Open Network → Interfaces and record the device and address of lan.
2. Open the bridge list, open br-lan and record its member ports. Confirm the ISP port is not among them.
3. Open wan and record the protocol and gateway.
4. Open Firewall → Zones and confirm a zone covers lan and a zone covers wan.
5. Open Network → DHCP and confirm a scope exists for device br-lan, with a pool that excludes the appliance address.
6. From a desk PC, open the admin UI on the LAN address. This is the session you keep alive during every later apply.

*Deliverable: three facts recorded — the logical name, the device, and the address plus WAN gateway. Every later module asks for one of them.*

**Lab 2 — Build a second LAN on a free port (25 minutes)**

1. Confirm eth2 is absent from every bridge.
2. Create bridge br-guest with eth2 as its only member. Spanning tree off, MTU 1500. Apply and confirm from the office PC.
3. Create logical interface guest, device br-guest, protocol Static, 192.168.70.1 / 255.255.255.0, gateway empty, Use default route off. Apply and confirm.
4. From a laptop on eth2 with a temporary 192.168.70.50/24, ping 192.168.70.1. Stop and fix if this fails.
5. Add firewall zone guest with a forward to wan. Apply the firewall and confirm that window.
6. Add a DHCP subnet for 192.168.70.0/24 on device br-guest, leaving 192.168.70.1 out of the pool.

**Lab 3 — Add a tagged server network (25 minutes)**

1. Create a VLAN: parent eth0, ID 10, name eth0.10. Apply and confirm from the office LAN.
2. Create logical interface servers on device eth0.10 at 192.168.50.1/24, gateway empty, Use default route off. Apply and confirm.
3. From a host the switch places in VLAN 10, ping 192.168.50.1. If it fails, match the VLAN ID on the switch before going further.
4. Add a DHCP scope on device eth0.10, then a firewall zone covering servers, then a forward from lan so a desk PC can open a connection to 192.168.50.10.

*Lab discussion point: eth0 may remain a member of br-lan while eth0.10 exists. Candidates should be able to explain why: the bridge carries the untagged office LAN, and VLAN 10 is a different device on the same cable.*

chapters.title: Knowledge Check
chapters.content: Ten questions. Pass mark 70% (7 of 10). Select your answer for each question, then submit to see your score.

questions.q: A DHCP scope form asks for a device. The office LAN is logical interface lan on bridge br-lan. What do you enter?
options: lan
br-lan
eth0
questions.explanation: DHCP binds the device name. Zones store the logical name; the two are different objects.

questions.q: Two cables run from the appliance to the same office switch and should behave as a single uplink. Which object do you create?
options: A VLAN on each port
A VRF containing both ports
A bond
Two logical interfaces with equal metrics
questions.explanation: A bond joins this appliance to one other switch over several cables as one link. A bridge joins hosts to each other.

questions.q: Where does the IP address live once a physical port has been made a member of a bridge?
options: On the physical port
On the bridge device itself
On the logical interface whose device is the bridge
On the firewall zone
questions.explanation: Once a port is a bridge member, the address for that network lives on the logical interface whose device is the bridge.

questions.q: An administrator applies a new LAN address, cannot reach the UI, and reboots the appliance during the confirmation window. What happens?
options: The previous address is restored by the rollback
The new design stays in place
The appliance boots with no address
Both addresses are kept as primary and secondary
questions.explanation: A reboot during the confirmation window does not roll the change back. The window must be allowed to expire.

questions.q: Which statement about a VRF is correct?
options: It decides which packets are permitted between networks
It is a routing table; ports assigned to it leave the table holding the office default gateway
Creating one automatically removes the matching firewall zone
It replaces the need for a logical interface on that port
questions.explanation: A VRF is a routing table; a firewall zone is policy. Creating a VRF leaves zones untouched.

questions.q: The wan row shows an address but no gateway. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The LAN cannot hand out DHCP leases
Internet traffic has nowhere to go, and Multi-WAN shows a link that cannot carry traffic
The firewall blocks all outbound sessions
The interface will roll back at the next reboot
questions.explanation: An address without a gateway means the circuit is up but the internet has no next hop.

questions.q: What is the valid range for a VLAN ID on this appliance?
questions.explanation: The ID is 1 through 4094, and it must match the number the switch tags.

questions.q: On the office LAN interface, the IPv4 gateway field is cleared and saved. At the next apply, what does the appliance do?
options: Keeps the previous gateway until it is replaced
Removes the previous gateway
Copies the gateway from wan
Rejects the save as incomplete
questions.explanation: Empty means removed: an empty gateway, DNS list or metric removes the previous value.

questions.q: A port is to be used only as a member of a bond. Which protocol belongs on it?
options: Static with a /32 address
DHCP
None (unmanaged)
PPPoE
questions.explanation: Protocol none (shown in some builds as unmanaged) is for a port that is only a bridge or bond member.

questions.q: Both an interface change and a firewall change are pending. What is the correct order?
options: Apply the firewall first, then the interface, confirming once at the end
Apply both, then confirm the single combined window
Confirm the interface window first from a path that still works, then apply the firewall and confirm its own window
Reboot, which commits both safely
questions.explanation: They are two separate windows. Confirm the interface first from a surviving path, then apply and confirm the firewall.

chapters.title: Key Terms
chapters.content:
| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Physical port | A socket on the appliance, such as eth0. |
| Device | The object packets are sent on: a bridge, a VLAN, a bond or a bare port. |
| Logical interface | The named binding of a device, a protocol and an address; the name other pages store. |
| Bridge | A device that makes several ports one broadcast domain. |
| VLAN | A tagged network on an existing port, identified by an ID from 1 to 4094. |
| Bond | Two or more ports used as a single link toward one switch or appliance. |
| VRF | A named routing table with a table id from 1 to 4294967294. |
| Confirmation window | The period after an Apply during which the change must be confirmed, or the previous design returns. |
| Use default route | The per-interface switch that allows that interface's gateway to become a candidate for the internet. |
| Metric | A route preference on a WAN; the lower metric wins while both circuits are up. |

chapters.title: Summary and What Comes Next
chapters.content:
- Four object kinds live on one screen: port, device, logical interface and VRF. Each has one job.
- The address belongs to the logical interface, never to a port that has joined a bridge or a bond.
- Other pages store different handles: zones and Multi-WAN store the logical name, DHCP stores the device, VPNs store the prefix.
- Every interface change is staged, applied, and then confirmed — and a reboot during the window does not undo it.
- Build in order: device, logical interface, reachability test, DHCP, firewall zone, DNS.

Module 02 moves to the devices themselves — bridges, VLANs and bonds — and builds the guest and server networks end to end. Module 03 covers DHCP and DNS services on top of the interfaces created here.
